Tracking PSX dividends and cash income

Dividends are income related to ownership — not the same event as selling shares. Recording them cleanly keeps Total Return, cash and tax-season stories honest. Here is how to think about dividend events inside PSX Tracker.

By PSX Tracker · Updated 23 September 2026

What to record on a dividend

Capture the date that matches your broker or company notice, the ticker, and the amount. If withholding appears on the statement, record it so net income stays explainable.

Use the share or fund book that actually held the position on the relevant date.

Cash versus reinvested

Cash dividends increase cash available in the account story. Reinvested dividends purchase more shares or fund units — income still happened, but cash may not sit idle.

If you only record cash and forget reinvested units, holdings drift away from the statement.

Withholding and informational totals

Brokers may deduct tax at source on dividends. Tracking that withholding helps you reconcile net credits and informational tax views later.

Your formal tax treatment still follows FBR rules and advisor guidance — the tracker is a ledger aid.

Where totals show up

Portfolio summaries typically separate dividend income from unrealized marks and realized trading gains. After dividend season, skim history and summary cards for surprises.

If a payout is missing, check whether you held the name through the required date and whether the event was imported or entered.

This guide is educational and describes how PSX Tracker works. It is not investment, tax or legal advice. Confirm rules and figures with your broker, FBR guidance and professional advisors.

Three different events that all get called a dividend

A cash dividend sends money. A bonus issue sends extra shares. A dividend reinvested at a fund sends extra units. They all come from a distribution announcement, and they do not belong in the same column. Cash increases the cash balance. Bonus shares increase quantity and usually change the cost per share. Reinvested units increase the fund holding.

Withholding tax is a fourth number. The company or the fund may pay you the net amount and remit tax on your behalf. If you record only the cash that arrived, you understate the dividend and you lose the tax already suffered. Record gross, tax, and net. The cash book should move by the net. The income book should show the gross.

Face value is part of the announcement when a company declares a percentage. “100 percent” means something different after a share splits or the face value changes. Read the notice for the face value it uses, and do not multiply a percentage by an old face value because a spreadsheet still has 10 in a cell.

Dates: announcement, book closure, and payment

You do not earn a dividend by owning the share on the day you hear the rumor. Companies announce a rate, a book-closure window, and later a payment. The holder on the register for that book closure is the person the company pays. Buying after you have missed that window does not catch the payout, even if the price has not yet fallen.

The ex-date idea is the market’s way of saying the new buyer will not receive this distribution. Prices often adjust. Your personal gain calculation should not treat that price drop as a mysterious loss if you also received the cash. The cash is in a different column. The shares you still hold are marked at the new price.

Payment can lag the announcement by weeks. Do not enter the cash on the announcement date unless the money is already in the broker wallet. Enter it when you receive it, and keep the announcement date in the note so you can match the company notice.

Bonus shares and the cost stack

Bonus shares are not free in the sense that your wealth doubled. You own more shares of the same company, and the price typically adjusts. For a personal FIFO book, you need a rule for the cost of the new shares. Many investors spread the existing cost across the new total quantity so the total cost does not jump. Write the rule down and apply it the same way every time.

A rights issue is different again. You pay for the new shares. That payment is a real cost and belongs in the new lot at the price you paid, plus charges. Ignoring the cheque and only adding the quantity makes every later sale look more profitable than it was.

If you skip the corporate action and only change the quantity to match the broker, the average cost on screen will be wrong even when the share count is right. Match both quantity and cost to the statement after every book closure you participated in.

Funds distribute differently from companies

An open-end fund may pay cash, issue bonus units, or both. Bonus units that restore the NAV after a distribution are often your own capital coming back as units, and the tax treatment is not the same as a cash dividend from a listed company. The fund’s statement and the category of the fund matter. Do not copy the share-dividend habit across.

Someone who wants the fund’s growth without the distribution will sometimes switch categories around an announcement. That is a tax-sensitive decision, not a tracker trick. Confirm it with an adviser. The app can record the switch you made. It should not recommend the switch.

MUFAP publishes NAVs. It does not tell you that you personally received a dividend. Your asset-manager statement does. Use the statement for the units and the cash, and the NAV only to mark what you still hold.

Where the money shows up in a portfolio

Total return is price change plus income, minus what you paid away in costs and taxes. A portfolio that ignores dividends will look worse than the investor’s actual result, especially for companies that pay a large share of their return in cash. A portfolio that counts the dividend and also counts a withdrawal of that same cash as a loss will look worse twice.

In PSX Tracker, a cash dividend increases cash. It is not a capital gain and it is not a deposit of new savings. A withdrawal is you taking cash out. Keeping those three events apart is what makes “how much did I invest?” a different number from “what is the account worth?”

Once a quarter, list the dividends you think you were owed and tick them against the bank or broker credits. Missed dividends are usually a book-closure date you misunderstood, a bonus you recorded as cash, or a fund distribution you never entered. The export-and-reconcile guide is the checklist for that afternoon.

Common questions

Should I record a dividend as cash or as new shares?

Cash dividends increase cash. A reinvested or bonus issue changes units or shares. Record the one that actually happened.

Where does withholding tax go?

Record tax withheld separately from the gross dividend so income and cash both stay explainable.

Does the tracker know every PSX dividend automatically?

Upcoming dividend research can suggest payouts. Your ledger still needs the dividend you actually received.
